name: Fantastical
tagline: Create a polished Apple calendar client with natural-language event entry and local sets

pricing.notes: Based on annual individual billing divided by 12; monthly and regional prices differ.

tiers.limits: 1 calendar set, 2 weeks of calendar mirroring, 3-day weather, 1 invitee/event and Meet With for 1 person; no Openings/Proposals/RSVP

tiers.limits: 1 person; unlimited calendar sets/invitees/Meet With, 6-month mirroring, 10-day weather and all Fantastical Scheduling features

tiers.name: Family
tiers.limits: Up to 5 family members with the full Individual feature set
tiers.notes: US App Store lists $89.99/year, which rounds to $7.50/month.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Teams of any size; Individual features plus SSO and multi-host Openings
tiers.notes: The current official page lists monthly and annual billing but its dynamic team price was not exposed reliably, so both values are null.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 calendar set, 2 weeks mirroring, 3-day weather, 1 invitee/event and Meet With for 1 person; no Fantastical Scheduling Openings/Proposals/RSVP
pricing.hiddenCosts: Team is per user; Family is a flat plan for up to 5 people. App-store taxes and regional prices can differ. Mid-cycle upgrades are prorated; education and military discounts require verification.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Fantastical, create a polished Apple calendar client with natural-language event entry and local sets. The hard boundary is native apple integrations, widgets, sync, proposals, and years of calendar edge cases, plus calendar integrations and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Type an event in plain language, see how it was understood, confirm, and have it land in the calendar you already use.
whatYouLose: native Apple integrations, widgets, sync, proposals, and years of calendar edge cases
a real month and week grid you can drag events around in
travel time, weather and conference call detection
ongoingBurden: OAuth refresh, webhooks, timezone databases, race conditions, reminders, deliverability, privacy, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Fantastical because people pay because one double booking or missed invite can cost more than years of subscription fees. The recurring cost buys OAuth refresh, webhooks, timezone databases, race conditions, reminders, deliverability, privacy, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

prompt:
Build me a natural-language quick-entry tool for my calendar, to replace Fantastical.
Use exactly this stack: Node 22 + TypeScript + chrono-node for parsing + tsdav for CalDAV; no alternative stacks.
Primary job: type "dentist tuesday 2:30 to 3:15" and have a real event appear in the calendar I already own, after I have seen how the sentence was read.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
A command quick "..." parses date, start, duration, location after "at" or "in", and a calendar picked with /work or /personal.
Always print the parsed result as a plain sentence and wait for confirmation before writing. A quick-entry tool that guesses silently is worse than a form.
Warn when the new event overlaps an existing one, and name what it collides with.
Connect over CalDAV to iCloud or Google using an app password from .env. The provider calendar stays the single source of truth · keep no local event database.
A command agenda prints today and tomorrow as a compact list.
Recurrence for the cases people actually type: every monday, every other week, first friday of the month. Anything more exotic is refused with a clear message rather than guessed.
Handle the timezone honestly: parse in the local zone, store in UTC, and show the zone in the confirmation line whenever it differs from the machine.
A menu bar window with a single input field is the finishing touch. Build it after the CLI works, with Tauri.
Do not add accounts, telemetry, or a hosted service.
Include clear empty, loading, success and recoverable error states, especially when CalDAV is unreachable.
Write focused tests for the parser: relative days, times without minutes, ranges, and the recurrence cases above.
Create a README with CalDAV setup for iCloud and Google, and the parser's known limits.
Deliberately out of scope: a month grid view, invitations and attendee management, and any booking page for other people.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than describing them.
